messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 53-year-old married North American man who has spent most of his adult life working predictable routes as a bus driver, someone used to long hours, early starts, and the steady rhythm of people getting on and off his vehicle. He described the traumatic event as a sexual assault that took place after an exhausting shift, at a point when he was so tired he felt dulled and slow, more focused on getting through the end of the day than on anything around him. In the account he gave, what remained most vivid was not only the assault itself but the sense of being trapped with another person in close quarters, aware of sounds around him and unable to stop what was happening to his body. When he speaks about it now, the memory does not come to him as something distant or softened by time. It arrives with the same terror he felt then, as if the event is happening again rather than being remembered. He says it is like a film that starts playing without his permission, scene by scene, and once it begins he cannot easily interrupt it.

In the weeks that followed, David tried to put the assault away and continue working. From the outside he looked as though he had returned to routine, but internally he found himself bracing against moments that felt dangerously close to that night. Fatigue became one of the strongest of these moments. If he was very tired or physically worn down, he noticed an immediate shift in himself, as though exhaustion made him vulnerable again. On those days, climbing into the driver's seat before dawn or late in a long shift could fill him with dread. He had come to regard tiredness itself as unsafe. Related sounds could affect him just as sharply. Certain noises in or around the bus, especially when they came suddenly and he was already strained, would bring the memory back with terrifying force. He did not experience these as ordinary reminders. For him, the sounds seemed to collapse time.

Driving with other people on board, once simply the structure of his workday, also became hard to bear. The presence of passengers behind him or near him altered his sense of safety. He found himself acutely aware of bodies in the bus, of movement, voices, and small sounds, and at times he would feel the memory beginning to unspool while he was still trying to complete his route. He did not tell coworkers exactly why this was happening. What felt most unbearable was the shame. When the memory returned, it brought not only terror but an intense sense of humiliation about what had happened to his body. He spoke about this haltingly, with his eyes down, as if even putting it into words risked exposing something degrading. He had come to believe that what happened had permanently changed how he saw himself.

Over time, this altered how he looked at other people as well. David said plainly that he no longer believes people can be trusted. The conviction sits broadly in his life now, extending beyond the person who assaulted him. He described feeling that his faith in people, in life, and in anything larger that might once have made the world feel ordered had fallen away. He does not offer this dramatically; rather, it appears in the flat certainty with which he expects disappointment, harm, or betrayal. At home, this has left him more closed with his wife. He has not felt able to let her fully see what the memories contain or how ashamed he feels, and the distance between them has become another quiet consequence of the assault. At work, he has increasingly dreaded shifts when he is already depleted, knowing that fatigue, passenger presence, or certain sounds on the bus may corner him with the same terror all over again.

By the time he sought help, David was living with the sense that the event was never fully over, only waiting to be replayed. What finally brought him in was not a single new incident so much as the accumulation of this cycle in the middle of ordinary life: driving while exhausted, hearing a sound, feeling the film begin again, and being flooded with terror and shame while trying to keep going. He wants relief from the replaying and from the sense that his body is marked by what happened. What frightens him most is the possibility that this is now permanent—that he will go on distrusting everyone, shrinking from other people around him, and feeling the same terror every time the memory returns.
